summary: Vandalizer has useful workflow primitives, clear source-oriented chat, and substantial validation transparency. Its interface is held back by competing panels, inconsistent visual treatments, cramped metadata, and several concrete interaction defects. Prioritize reliable task completion and responsive layout before adding more onboarding or decorative UI.
rubric: Scores are Codex-authored judgments from screenshots and exercised frontend interactions, not automated design measurements or user-research results. Visual UI considers hierarchy, spacing, typography, consistency, contrast, and layout. UX considers discoverability, task progression, feedback, recovery, and scope clarity. Both use 0–10: 9–10 exceptional; 8 strong; 7 usable with polish needed; 6 recurring friction; 5 substantial problems; below 5 a core task is compromised. The combined grade is 40% UI + 60% UX. Section grades emphasize desktop; the separate mobile grade applies across the product. No production usage weighting is claimed.
scope: Current React source served by Vite, with a fresh production build for the validation results and critical interaction rechecks. Synthetic authenticated account, team, documents, projects, automations, library items, KB sources, validation data and chat/tool streams. Desktop 1440×1000 and mobile 390×844, Chromium headless, device scale 1. All /api requests are intercepted. No real documents, accounts, automations, messages, model calls, or production records were created or modified.
limitations: This grades frontend presentation and interaction, not model quality, retrieval accuracy, backend ingestion, authorization, tool execution, job reliability, or validation mathematics. Agent and validation results are explicit fixtures. Live streaming/stop/reconnect, large libraries, alternate roles/themes, M365 intake, schedule/API wizard branches, validation apply/revert and cross-browser behavior remain untested. The first-run tour overlay is dismissed consistently; the basic first-session chat surface is covered. Accessibility findings are automated signals plus visual inspection, not a complete accessibility conformance audit.

areas.name: File browser
areas.strength: Familiar table, explicit selection, a visible upload target, and useful bulk/context actions. Selecting a file exposes its scope in chat and replaces the generic welcome panel with relevant prompts.
areas.critique: The heading says PDFs while the uploader supports eight extensions. Oversized upload space pushes the list downward; pale timestamps and file-type hints are hard to read. On mobile, filenames are reduced to a few characters. The useful row menu is visually hover-dependent.
areas.recommendation: Use Files as the heading, make upload a compact action, allocate width to filenames, and retain a persistent accessible action menu. Put size/type limits next to upload and make row status legible.

areas.name: Projects
areas.strength: Compact cards, readable titles, useful state badges, and a sensible explanation of what belongs in a project. Opening a project creates a visible project context.
areas.critique: Six small icon/count pairs require interpretation; the create action is an unlabeled plus button. The list has no visible search or sorting. The empty state is lengthy while creation remains a small control at the top.
areas.recommendation: Name the create action, expose labeled counts for the most useful objects, add search/sort for growth, and make the primary project task prominent. Keep the project explanation short enough to act on immediately.

areas.name: Automations screen and editor
areas.strength: Trigger filters, action names, and an obvious New action make a short automation list easy to scan. The editor makes enabled/private status explicit and provides Run now.
areas.critique: List status is a tiny colored dot rather than a clear Enabled/Paused label. The dark list and white editor feel like separate products. A normal title wraps to three lines in the narrow editor, while operational information such as last outcome is absent from the list.
areas.recommendation: Show Enabled/Paused, last outcome and next run where relevant; give the editor more width; group trigger → input → action → output in a compact summary before the detailed settings.

areas.name: Automation creation wizard
areas.strength: The five-step folder-watch path has clear required fields, readable choice cards, useful defaults, and a good library picker. Disabled Next prevents skipping the required folder/action.
areas.critique: Pressing Enter in the description field dismissed the dialog in the controlled run. The final screen defaults to Enable immediately but does not restate the selected folder, filters, and workflow. Numbered progress lacks descriptive step names; blue controls introduce another palette.
areas.recommendation: Fix keyboard progression and focus handling first. Add a final review of name, trigger, input, action, output and activation. Offer Save disabled and Create & enable as explicit choices, and label the steps.

areas.name: Knowledge bases
areas.strength: Sources are inspectable; failed sources show the error and Try again. Ownership/sharing actions and source-refresh controls are available. The trust banner explains why evaluation matters.
areas.critique: Ready dominates even when one of three sources failed. Chunks and source counts are tiny and low contrast. The page carries too many equal-weight actions before the validation task. Cards and source rows contain nested interactive controls; the list sort has no accessible name.
areas.recommendation: Separate availability, source completeness, and measured quality. Lead with 2 of 3 sources ready — 1 needs attention. Put sources and validation in clearly labeled primary views; move secondary management actions into a menu and fix the interaction semantics.

areas.name: KB validation system
areas.strength: The tuning wizard previews expected answers, distinguishes a no-KB baseline, states budget/time, and leaves automatic application off by default. Run now, Test Queries and History support different jobs. Result views explicitly distinguish composite quality from answer accuracy.
areas.critique: Validation starts far down the source-management page. Users must learn Validate, Run now, Test Queries, tuning, baseline and token budgets. The six-step wizard opens with substantial technical explanation and ends with disabled coming-in-v2 controls. Budget recommendations sound more certain than a tiny evaluation set warrants.
areas.recommendation: Offer two clear tasks: Check answer quality and Improve retrieval. Show scope, sample size, expected time and cost before starting; keep technical controls optional. Preserve the expected-answer preview, explicit score formula and manual apply step. Remove unavailable controls from the primary path.

areas.name: Explore / shared catalog
areas.strength: Cards show type, measured quality, sample count and adoption. Detail views have a clear Save to Library action. Search, quality and sort filters support discovery.
areas.critique: The entry point is Everyone, while other copy says catalog, making location less predictable. Library search and catalog search coexist. The knowledge catalog adds a wide All Knowledge Bases sidebar to an already constrained panel. Secondary trust metadata is very small, and the modal switches from Checked to Verified terminology.
areas.recommendation: Choose one stable navigation label, such as Explore, and explain sharing scope beneath it. Use a single contextual search. Collapse the catalog sidebar when it contains only one option. Standardize trust vocabulary and emphasize fit, required inputs, provenance and limitations.

areas.name: Library
areas.strength: Useful Mine/Team scope, type filters, favorites, pins and folders. The empty state has concrete create/browse actions rather than just an illustration.
areas.critique: The first populated item is visibly clipped below the Name header. Secondary metadata has multiple contrast failures. The stacked scope/filter/sidebar controls consume space; at 390px the sidebar leaves item names nearly unreadable. Users must also distinguish pinning, favoriting, folders and projects.
areas.recommendation: Fix the item/header geometry and responsive layout first. Collapse saved views into a mobile menu, give names the full width, and reduce competing organization concepts on the initial view. Keep frequently used tools and search prominent.

areas.name: Chat workspace
areas.strength: The actual conversation layout is restrained and readable, with strong distinction between user and assistant, a stable composer, and visible source chips.
areas.critique: The returning-user home is a large promotional gradient with duplicate Ask about current work actions and several layers of prompts. It competes with the active work panel on other screens. The empty Activity rail reserves substantial desktop width. At narrow width, the composer occupies an excessive portion of the screen.
areas.recommendation: Use a compact task launcher and recent work, move certification out of the main task hierarchy, and collapse empty Activity by default. Open the assistant contextually beside an active task, with an obvious way to expand it.

areas.name: Basic chat onboarding
areas.strength: Upload a document and Run sample demo are concrete starting points. A clearly labeled demo preview shows an answer alongside supporting evidence.
areas.critique: The screen is much closer to a landing page than a first working session. Multiple paragraphs explain the design strategy, and certification competes with the first useful action. The promise that every answer links to sources is broader than a general chat can always support.
areas.recommendation: Reduce the first session to one file or one demo, a suggested question and an inspectable answer. Move learning material below task completion. Describe sourced answers in terms of attached documents/KBs rather than an unconditional guarantee.

areas.name: Chat uploads
areas.strength: The Add menu clearly distinguishes document, website and knowledge-base inputs. Upload failures appear as dismissible alerts with a concrete reason.
areas.critique: A successful synthetic upload creates the file and shows a success toast, but its chat attachment is cleared. The next chat request submits document_uuids: []. This compromises the central upload → ask workflow even though the upload itself succeeded.
areas.recommendation: Make chat source selection authoritative and preserve it across file-list refreshes. Show a persistent file chip with uploading, processing, ready and failed states. Gate readiness explicitly and provide retry/remove. Add a regression test that asserts the next chat request contains the uploaded UUID.

areas.name: Chat knowledge-base interactions
areas.strength: Chat from a KB attaches visible scope, changes the introductory guidance, and renders source chips on the answer. Detach/share controls have meaningful accessible names.
areas.critique: The attached KB name truncates aggressively, even in a wide workspace. Source evidence uses small secondary text. The headline KB state does not bring failed-source coverage into the conversation.
areas.recommendation: Let the source-scope strip expand to show full names and readiness/coverage. Make source inspection a first-class action near the relevant claim. Verify live citation grounding separately before interpreting the fixture response as quality evidence.

areas.name: Agentic chat UI
areas.strength: The tested frontend renders a proposed change, Confirm/Cancel, a plan, completed steps, tool success and actionable tool errors. Confirmation submits Yes, go ahead, and prior confirmation controls disappear afterward.
areas.critique: Confirm is generic, and the proposed change has little visual separation from ordinary assistant text. A completed plan remains below a later failed tool turn in the fixture sequence, making its scope ambiguous. A completion message should offer a direct artifact action when the tool provides one.
areas.recommendation: Use action-specific approval labels and a structured change preview. Associate each plan with the turn or operation it describes, and distinguish waiting for approval, running, failed and completed. Provide Open workflow / View result next to completion.

findings.title: Successful chat upload loses its document scope
findings.detail: Upload through Add → Add Document. The fixture returns complete:true and doc-upload; the refreshed file list includes it. Submit a summary request. The captured request has document_uuids: []. FileBrowser emits its independent empty checkbox selection whenever documents change; LeftPanel forwards it into workspace selection. This is a frontend reproduction, not a claim about real ingestion.
findings.acceptance: After upload and every processing/list refresh, the file chip remains and the next chat request includes exactly the intended uploaded document UUID.

findings.title: Mobile shell overflows and Library becomes unusably narrow
findings.detail: All six 390px captures have a document width of 521px. The header extends beyond the viewport. Library keeps a desktop sidebar and two-column list, leaving very little room for item names; Files also truncates normal filenames severely.
findings.acceptance: At 390px and 320px, document width equals viewport width, key account/navigation controls remain reachable, and item names/actions are usable without horizontal page scrolling.

findings.title: Enter in automation description dismisses the wizard
findings.detail: Open New Automation, fill a name and the description, then press Enter in the description input. The dialog disappears instead of proceeding visibly. Reproduced in both development and the production preview. The window-level Enter handler and focus transition deserve inspection; the precise cause is not established by this audit.
findings.acceptance: Enter in the name/description step advances exactly once, preserves input and focus, and does not activate Close or dismiss the draft.

findings.title: Library clips the first item's name
findings.detail: At initial scroll position, the first row's title begins above the visible item area beneath the Name header. The mobile version amplifies the problem.
findings.acceptance: The complete first item title is visible at scrollTop 0 at desktop and narrow widths, with consistent row/header spacing.

findings.title: Welcome content outranks the task being performed
findings.detail: A large, repeated chat welcome card occupies roughly a third of desktop width beside each active section. A mostly empty Activity rail consumes additional width. The assistant dominates visually while the actual editor/list is compressed.
findings.acceptance: The selected workspace task receives the main canvas. Secondary panels open when relevant, and a compact assistant launcher replaces the repeated welcome hero.

findings.title: Status does not summarize operational completeness
findings.detail: Automation enabled/paused state relies on a tiny dot in the list. KB Ready remains prominent with a failed source. Availability, completeness and validation quality need distinct wording.
findings.acceptance: Automation cards include textual state. KB summary shows healthy/total sources and attention required independently of retrieval readiness and measured quality.

findings.title: Named controls, valid interaction structure and contrast need cleanup
findings.detail: Axe flags an unnamed Projects create button, an unnamed KB sort select, nested interactive KB cards/source rows, and low-contrast metadata. Examples include KB counts at 2.63:1 and Files timestamps at 2.67:1 in the captured theme. Counts across frames are repeated occurrences, not unique defects.
findings.acceptance: Controls have descriptive names, interactive children are not inside button ancestors, essential metadata meets contrast targets, and keyboard navigation is verified in each affected surface.

findings.title: Automation activation needs a concrete review step
findings.detail: The final step enables immediately by default but only summarizes activation/output. Users cannot verify the watched folder, file filters and chosen workflow together before enabling.
findings.acceptance: The final step states the complete trigger/input/action/output configuration and makes Save disabled versus Create & enable explicit.

findings.title: Validation asks users to learn too much before acting
findings.detail: A buried entry point, six wizard screens, technical retrieval vocabulary and token budgets create a high starting cost. Disabled future features occupy the final decision screen.
findings.acceptance: A short task-oriented path exposes sample quality, expected cost/time and scope, with optional technical detail. Unavailable future features are removed from the decision path.

findings.title: Agent progress needs clear operation scope
findings.detail: The fixture demonstrates readable tool feedback, but generic Confirm wording and a previously completed plan below a later failed tool turn leave room for ambiguity. This finding concerns frontend presentation of controlled events, not autonomous agent correctness.
findings.acceptance: Approval names the action and target; each plan/progress summary is visibly associated with its operation and cannot be mistaken for the status of a later failed turn.

repairOrder: Preserve upload-to-chat scope and fix wizard keyboard dismissal; add focused browser regression checks for those two user journeys.
Fix responsive header and Library/file-list geometry, including the clipped first row. Verify 390px, 320px and a common laptop viewport.
Give each workspace a primary canvas and make chat/activity contextual. Establish one shared color, spacing, type and control system.
Make operational status and activation review explicit. Separate ready, complete, checked and optimized states.
Resolve the measured accessibility issues, simplify onboarding/validation copy, and connect agent outcomes directly to the resulting artifacts.
